question: What is the primary target of a topical medication?
explanation: Topical medications are designed to be applied directly to external body surfaces like the skin or mucous membranes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why is the topical route preferred for localized skin infections?

options.A: It guarantees uniform distribution in the bloodstream
options.B: It speeds up complete absorption into deep tissues
options.C: It delivers a high concentration directly to the site
options.D: It requires the liver to metabolize the drug first

explanation: Applying drugs directly to the affected area concentrates the therapeutic agent where it is needed most while limiting systemic spread. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which topical formulation is best suited for dry, thick, or scaly skin lesions?
explanation: Ointments are oil-based and occlusive, making them effective at softening and treating dry, thick skin plaques. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h2)

question: What distinguishes a transdermal patch from a standard topical cream?

options.A: A patch is used exclusively for treating localized surface fungal infections
options.B: A patch delivers steady systemic absorption over a prolonged period
options.C: A patch remains completely impermeable to all active chemical substances
options.D: A patch requires daily removal and immediate reapplication every hour

explanation: Transdermal patches are engineered to bypass local skin treatment and provide continuous systemic drug delivery into the microvasculature. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h2)

question: Which layer of the skin serves as the primary barrier against drug absorption?
explanation: The outermost layer of the epidermis, the stratum corneum, resists foreign chemical penetration and limits drug absorption. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h3)

question: A patient with severe eczema has a steroid cream applied over a large area of broken skin. What is the main risk here?

options.C: Complete failure of the local treatment

explanation: Compromised skin integrity removes the natural barrier function, allowing topical drugs to enter the bloodstream rapidly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary reason for cleansing a skin wound before applying a new topical medication?

options.A: To permanently numb the underlying nerve endings
options.B: To remove residual medication and debris
options.C: To permanently seal the blood vessels shut
options.D: To stimulate rapid production of new skin cells

explanation: Cleansing clears away old ointment, exudate, and debris so the fresh medication can make direct contact with the target tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why must a nurse inspect the skin integrity before applying a medicated patch?

options.A: To assess the depth of the subcutaneous fat layer
options.B: To measure the exact surface temperature of the limb
options.C: To confirm the site is free of irritation or breakdown
options.D: To determine the patient's blood pressure baseline

explanation: Applying adhesive patches over broken or irritated skin causes pain, impairs drug absorption, and worsens skin damage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h4)

question: In which direction should a nurse apply a topical ointment on a patient's limb?

options.C: Against the natural grain of hair
options.D: In the direction of hair growth

explanation: Smoothing ointments along the direction of hair growth prevents painful inflammation of the hair follicles, known as folliculitis. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h5)

question: How should a nurse retrieve a dose of cream from a multi-use jar safely?

options.A: Dip gloved fingers directly into the container
options.B: Pour sterile water into the jar to liquefy it
options.C: Use a clean tongue depressor or applicator
options.D: Scrape the bottom with an unsterilized pen

explanation: Using a clean tool prevents microbial contamination of the remaining medication inside the shared multi-use container. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h5)

question: Which local reaction is commonly associated with an adverse response to a topical cream?
explanation: Itching, redness, and burning at the application site are typical signs of skin irritation or contact dermatitis. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is a known consequence of prolonged, high-potency topical steroid use on the skin?
explanation: Long-term steroid application breaks down collagen and dermal structures, leading to visible skin thinning and fragility. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h6)

question: What instruction should a nurse give a patient regarding the thickness of topical cream application?

options.A: Apply a thick coating to speed up the healing
options.B: Massage the cream until it completely disappears
options.C: Apply only a thin, even layer as prescribed
options.D: Reapply every hour regardless of the schedule

explanation: Thick layers waste medication and do not increase therapeutic benefits, and may increase the risk of adverse local reactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h7)

question: Why is hand hygiene emphasized after a patient applies a medicated skin ointment?

options.A: To remove natural oils from the surface of the palms
options.B: To cool down the hands after touching warm ointment
options.C: To ensure the skin on the fingers stays moisturized
options.D: To prevent accidental transfer of medication to the eyes

explanation: Washing hands removes residual active drugs, preventing accidental contact with sensitive mucous membranes like the eyes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h7)
